claim: Open research data provide considerable scientific, societal, and economic benefits.
source: Open research data provide considerable scientific, societal, and economic benefits.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Arzberger et al., 2004; Munafò et al., 2017; Murdoch and Detsky, 2013; Piwowar et al., 2011) as indicated in the full text.

claim: Disclosure risks can sometimes limit the sharing of open data, especially in datasets that include sensitive details or information from individuals with rare disorders.
source: However, disclosure risks can sometimes limit the sharing of open data, especially in datasets that include sensitive details or information from individuals with rare disorders.
evidence: This is a general statement about data sharing challenges, drawing on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Synthetic datasets were originally developed to permit the sharing of confidential census data.
source: This article introduces the concept of synthetic datasets, which is an emerging method originally developed to permit the sharing of confidential census data.
evidence: Supported by citations in the full text (Little, 1993; Reiter, 2005b; Reiter, 2005a; Reiter and Raghunathan, 2007; Rubin, 1993) and summary reference (Bonnéry et al., 2019).

claim: Synthetic datasets mimic real datasets by preserving their statistical properties and the relationships between variables.
source: Synthetic datasets mimic real datasets by preserving their statistical properties and the relationships between variables.
evidence: This is a definitional claim about synthetic datasets, supported by citations (Little, 1993; Reiter, 2005b; Reiter, 2005a; Reiter and Raghunathan, 2007; Rubin, 1993) in the full text.

claim: Synthetic datasets reduce disclosure risk to essentially nil as no record in the synthetic dataset represents a real individual.
source: Importantly, this method also reduces disclosure risk to essentially nil as no record in the synthetic dataset represents a real individual.
evidence: Supported by citation (Duncan and Elliot, 2011) in the full text.

claim: With open data, scholars can verify results, generate new knowledge, form new hypotheses, and reduce the unnecessary duplication of data collection.
source: With open data, scholars can verify results, generate new knowledge, form new hypotheses, and reduce the unnecessary duplication of data collection (Asendorpf et al., 2013; Nosek et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Researchers who wish to share data while reducing the risk of disclosure have traditionally used data anonymization procedures, in which explicit identifiers such as names, addresses, and national identity numbers are removed.
source: Researchers who wish to share data while reducing the risk of disclosure have traditionally used data anonymization procedures, in which explicit identifiers such as names, addresses, and national identity numbers are removed (Hrynaszkiewicz et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Specific individuals can still be identified in anonymized datasets with high accuracy despite anonymization efforts.
source: Despite these anonymization efforts, specific individuals can still be identified in anonymized datasets with high accuracy (Ohm, 2009; Rocher et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Data aggregation and random noise can distort the relationships between variables in the dataset, which can interfere with reproducibility and exploratory data analysis.
source: Data aggregation and random noise can also distort the relationships between variables in the dataset (Purdam and Elliot, 2007), which can interfere with reproducibility and exploratory data analysis.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work and logical inference about the consequences.

claim: The creation of synthetic datasets can substantially overcome replicability issues by creating a new dataset that mimics an original dataset by preserving its statistical properties and relationships between variables.
source: The creation of synthetic datasets can substantially overcome replicability issues, as this method creates a new dataset that mimics an original dataset by preserving its statistical properties and relationships between variables (Little, 1993; Reiter, 2005b; Reiter, 2005a; Reiter and Raghunathan, 2007; Rubin, 1993).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Synthetic datasets reduce disclosure risk to essentially zero, as no complete casewise record in the new dataset represents a real individual.
source: Synthetic datasets also reduce disclosure risk to essentially zero, as no complete casewise record in the new dataset represents a real individual (Duncan and Elliot, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Synthetic datasets allow researchers to fit exploratory models in the synthetic datasets, which the data custodians can verify in the original data.
source: Synthetic datasets also allow researchers to fit exploratory models in the synthetic datasets, which the data custodians can verify in the original data.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the utility of synthetic datasets based on their properties.

claim: Synthetic datasets enable readers and reviewers to better understand the data, as they can recreate the reported analyses and explore data distributions, variance, outliers, and means.
source: Finally, synthetic datasets enable readers and reviewers to better understand the data, as they can recreate the reported analyses and explore data distributions, variance, outliers, and means.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the benefits of synthetic datasets for transparency.

claim: Synthetic datasets were originally developed for sharing sensitive population-level data.
source: Synthetic datasets were originally developed for sharing sensitive population-level data (for a summary, see Bonnéry et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to a summary work.

claim: The use of synthetic data for sharing sensitive information is beginning to emerge in the biobehavioural sciences.
source: The use of synthetic data for sharing sensitive information is beginning to emerge in the biobehavioural sciences (e.g., Arslan et al., 2018; Newbury et al., 2018); however, this approach is not widely known in the field.
evidence: Supported by citations to examples in the field.

claim: The R script and datasets to reproduce the analyses described in this paper are available online at https://github.com/dsquintana/synthpop-primer.
source: The R script and datasets to reproduce the analyses described in this paper are available online at https://github.com/dsquintana/synthpop-primer (Quintana, 2019; copy archived at https://github.com/elifesciences-publications/synthpop-primer).
evidence: This is a direct statement about data availability.

claim: Synthetic datasets are created by replacing some or all of the data by sampling from an appropriate probability distribution, in a similar fashion to multiple imputation.
source: Synthetic datasets are created by replacing some or all of the data by sampling from an appropriate probability distribution, in a similar fashion to multiple imputation (Drechsler, 2011; Raghunathan et al., 2003; Reiter, 2005b).
evidence: Supported by citations to methodological work.

claim: The default synthesis method in synthpop is the classification and regression tree (CART) procedure.
source: The default synthesis method in synthpop is the classification and regression tree (CART) procedure (Reiter, 2005b), which will be used in this primer.
evidence: Supported by citation to methodological work.

claim: The CART procedure is more flexible and generally performs better than other synthesis methods, such as random forests and bagging.
source: The CART procedure is more flexible and generally performs better than other synthesis methods, such as random forests and bagging (Drechsler and Reiter, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to comparative methodological work.

claim: If data synthesis happens to recreate a replicate of a real individual by chance, these replicates can be easily identified and removed from the dataset to reduce the risk of de-identification.
source: If data synthesis happens to recreate a replicate of a real individual by chance, these replicates can be easily identified and removed from the dataset to reduce the risk of de-identification.
evidence: This is a logical inference about how to handle replicates in synthetic data.

claim: There are two broad approaches for assessing the utility of a synthesized dataset: general utility and specific utility.
source: There are two broad approaches for assessing the utility of a synthesized dataset: general utility and specific utility (Snoke et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to methodological work.

claim: General utility reflects the overall similarities in the statistical properties and multivariate relationships between the synthetic and original datasets.
source: General utility reflects the overall similarities in the statistical properties and multivariate relationships between the synthetic and original datasets.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about general utility.

claim: The first step in assessing general utility is data visualisation.
source: The first step in assessing general utility is data visualisation (Nowok et al., 2016; Raab et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to methodological work.

claim: The compare() function in synthpop can be used to construct side-by-side univariate distributions of variables in the synthetic and observed datasets.
source: The compare() function in synthpop can be used to construct side-by-side univariate distributions of variables in the synthetic and observed datasets.
evidence: This is a statement about the functionality of the synthpop package.

claim: Visualizing bivariate comparisons between specific variables of interest is recommended, as two datasets might have similar statistical properties despite different distributions.
source: Visualizing bivariate comparisons between specific variables of interest is also recommended, as two datasets might have similar statistical properties despite different distributions (e.g., Anscombe's quartet; Anscombe, 1973).
evidence: Supported by citation to a classic example (Anscombe's quartet).

claim: Confirming general utility is a necessary step for making inferences from the synthetic dataset and is especially important for data exploration in the synthetic dataset.
source: Confirming general utility is a necessary step for making inferences from the synthetic dataset and is especially important for data exploration in the synthetic dataset (Snoke et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to methodological work.

claim: Specific utility for fitted synthetic models can be assessed by calculating the lack-of-fit against the same model in the original data.
source: Specific utility for fitted synthetic models can be assessed by calculating the lack-of-fit against the same model in the original data (Nowok et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to methodological work.

claim: Specific coefficients in synthetic models can be compared against coefficients in the original models by assessing the differences in standardized coefficients and confidence interval (CI) overlap.
source: Specific coefficients in synthetic models can also be compared against coefficients in the original models by assessing the differences in standardized coefficients and confidence interval (CI) overlap (Karr et al., 2006), which is the ratio of the overlap of the intervals to an average of their lengths.
evidence: Supported by citation to methodological work.

claim: Higher overlap is indicative of greater specific utility, which suggests that inference from fitted synthetic models is valid.
source: Higher overlap is indicative of greater specific utility, which suggests that inference from fitted synthetic models is valid.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the interpretation of CI overlap.

claim: Synthetic datasets prepared for export will have a single string 'FAKE_DATA' variable added to the front of the dataset using the sdc() function in synthpop to remove any possible confusion.
source: Thus, to remove any possible confusion, synthetic datasets prepared for export will have a single string 'FAKE_DATA' variable added to the front of the dataset using the sdc() function in synthpop, as recommended by Nowok et al. (2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to a recommendation.
